messages.author: e8cf038997c431ea
messages.subject: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
parts:
Hi,

Attempting to implement a zero-inflated negative binomial model, analogous to the zeroinfl() command from the pscl package. Code attached. I'm (very) new to Stan, so any help would be much appreciated.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
parts:
Hi Kenneth, 

A few tips:

1) You want to use neg_binomial_2_log_log instead of neg_binomial_2_log. The names are unfortunate, but the former allows you to keep your linear predictor on the log scale. We really need to change the names because neg_binomial_2_log does seem like what you want but you need the extra _log at the end. 

2) In your simulations you say that z is the logit regressor but in your model both x and z are used in the negative binomial rather than the bernoulli. Typically you'd use the same predictors (x in this case) in both calls to the negative binomial distribution and use z in a model for the bernoulli parameter theta. To do this, theta doesn't need to be declared as a parameter (just d0 and d1) and then you can construct theta in the model block, since it would be a deterministic function of d0, d1 and the data z. On a related note, I noticed that that the d0 and d1 parameters don't factor into your simulations of the data. I would generate z from a normal distribution and then compute inv_logit(d0 + d1 * z) and use that as the probabilities for the bernoulli in your simulations instead of just taking z from a uniform(0,1). 

3) For both theoretical and computational reasons we recommend much tighter priors than normal(0,500), which gives non-negligible weight to values like -1000 and 1000. For your example you probably don't need anything wider than normal(0, 5), and you could probably even go tighter than that. 

Hope that helps, 

Jonah

parts:
Hi Jonah,

Thanks for the helpful reply. It runs and seems to perform well. However, I still get errors like the following.

I've noticed similar errors in other GLMs - even when they appear to be working correctly. Any idea what may be causing this?

Revised model code below:

model_code <- '

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;    
  real X[N,K];
  int<lower=0> Y[N];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> phi;
  real b0;
  real b1;
  real d0;
  real d1;
}


model {
  #priors:
  phi ~ normal(0,5);
  b0 ~ normal(0,5);
  b1 ~ normal(0,5);
  d0 ~ normal(0,5);
  d1 ~ normal(0,5);

  #data model:
  for (n in 1:N) {
    if (Y[n] == 0)
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
                                      bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
                                      + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
    else
      increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
                          + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));

  }  
 }
'

messages.subject: Re: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
parts:
Hi Kenneth, that message you're seeing is more of a warning than an error, and you'll often get a few of these during warmup when you have parameters with constraints. But that's ok. As long as you're not getting a ton of them after the warmup period and you're getting good results (e.g. recovering the parameters from the fake data simulation, etc.) then you're fine.

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
parts:
What's going on is that Stan's using a default step size to start,
and then uses the posterior gradient, which is only a linear approximation
to the curvature. The problem is that it can cause us to step over a boundary.
Starting with smaller step sizes tends to help reduce these warnings at the
cost of more run time.

Michael's teaching us to be worried if there is even one such warning
(reported as divergent iterations --- the divergence is that there's not
a finite log density) in the sampling part of the run.

You usually don't want to recompute expressions. So this:

> for (n in 1:N) {
> if (Y[n] == 0)
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
> bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> else
> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
would be a bit more efficient as
> for (n in 1:N) {

real temp;
temp <- d0 + d1 * X[n,1];
> if (Y[n] == 0)

> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1, temp),
> bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)

> + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> else
> increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)
> + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));

but probably wouldn't be noticeable. You could make it even faster by defining
a vector on the outside and access it as:

{
vector[N] temp;
temp <- d0 + d1 * col(X, 1);

... replace temp above with temp[n] ...

Same for b0 and b1. And it's more efficient if you declare X as an
array of vectors, so that the equivalent of col() is constant time.

- Bob

parts:
To follow up on Bob's comment about stepsize, since you're using RStan you can add the 'control' argument (a named list) to your call to the stan(). You can either directly manipulate stepsize using 

control = list(stepsize = value)

or alternatively you can increase the target metropolis acceptance rate using 

control = list(adapt_delta = value), 

which will also lead to a smaller stepsize. The default for adapt_delta is 0.8, so you could try setting it to .9 or even higher and it should help avoid those warnings. 

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial
parts:
And you can do both. If you set the stepsize lower, it helps
during warmup not have errors and if you set target acceptance
higher, it makes things more stable. Calling this a "Metropolis"
accept rate is misleading --- it's an average acceptance rate from
points on the HMC trajectory in NUTS's slice sampler.

- Bob

> On Oct 20, 2015, at 6:03 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> To follow up on Bob's comment about stepsize, since you're using RStan you can add the 'control' argument (a named list) to your call to the stan(). You can either directly manipulate stepsize using
>
> control = list(stepsize = value)
>
> or alternatively you can increase the target metropolis acceptance rate using
>
> control = list(adapt_delta = value),
>
> which will also lead to a smaller stepsize. The default for adapt_delta is 0.8, so you could try setting it to .9 or even higher and it should help avoid those warnings.
>
> Jonah
>
> On Tuesday, October 20, 2015, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> What's going on is that Stan's using a default step size to start,
> and then uses the posterior gradient, which is only a linear approximation
> to the curvature. The problem is that it can cause us to step over a boundary.
> Starting with smaller step sizes tends to help reduce these warnings at the
> cost of more run time.
>
> Michael's teaching us to be worried if there is even one such warning
> (reported as divergent iterations --- the divergence is that there's not
> a finite log density) in the sampling part of the run.
>
> You usually don't want to recompute expressions. So this:
>
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> > if (Y[n] == 0)
> > increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
> > bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> > else
> > increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
>
> would be a bit more efficient as
>
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> real temp;
> temp <- d0 + d1 * X[n,1];
> > if (Y[n] == 0)
> > increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1, temp),
> > bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> > else
> > increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0, temp)
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
>
>
> but probably wouldn't be noticeable. You could make it even faster by defining
> a vector on the outside and access it as:
>
> {
> vector[N] temp;
> temp <- d0 + d1 * col(X, 1);
>
> ... replace temp above with temp[n] ...
>
> Same for b0 and b1. And it's more efficient if you declare X as an
> array of vectors, so that the equivalent of col() is constant time.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Oct 20, 2015, at 4:04 PM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Kenneth, that message you're seeing is more of a warning than an error, and you'll often get a few of these during warmup when you have parameters with constraints. But that's ok. As long as you're not getting a ton of them after the warmup period and you're getting good results (e.g. recovering the parameters from the fake data simulation, etc.) then you're fine.
> >
> > Jonah
> >
> > On Tuesday, October 20, 2015 at 2:53:26 PM UTC-4, Kenneth Lowande wrote:
> > Hi Jonah,
> >
> > Thanks for the helpful reply. It runs and seems to perform well. However, I still get errors like the following.
> >
> >
> >
> > I've noticed similar errors in other GLMs - even when they appear to be working correctly. Any idea what may be causing this?
> >
> > Revised model code below:
> >
> > model_code <- '
> >
> > data {
> > int<lower=1> N;
> > int<lower=1> K;
> > real X[N,K];
> > int<lower=0> Y[N];
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> > real<lower=0> phi;
> > real b0;
> > real b1;
> > real d0;
> > real d1;
> > }
> >
> >
> > model {
> > #priors:
> > phi ~ normal(0,5);
> > b0 ~ normal(0,5);
> > b1 ~ normal(0,5);
> > d0 ~ normal(0,5);
> > d1 ~ normal(0,5);
> >
> > #data model:
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> > if (Y[n] == 0)
> > increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1,d0 + d1 * X[n,1]),
> > bernoulli_logit_log(0, d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2],phi)));
> > else
> > increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,d0 + d1 * X[n,1])
> > + neg_binomial_2_log_log(Y[n], b0 + b1 * X[n,2], phi));
> >
> > }
> > }
> > '
> >
> >
> > On Monday, October 19, 2015 at 5:14:57 PM UTC-4, Jonah wrote:
> > Also, if you do end making theta a linear predictor then you can use bernoulli_logit_log instead of bernoulli_log because theta will then be on the logit scale. If you use bernoulli_log you'll need to compute inv_logit(theta) whereas bernoulli_logit_log will do that for you and will be more computationally stable.
> >
> > On Monday, October 19, 2015 at 5:12:28 PM UTC-4, Jonah wrote:
> > Hi Kenneth,
> >
> > A few tips:
> >
> > 1) You want to use neg_binomial_2_log_log instead of neg_binomial_2_log. The names are unfortunate, but the former allows you to keep your linear predictor on the log scale. We really need to change the names because neg_binomial_2_log does seem like what you want but you need the extra _log at the end.
> >
> > 2) In your simulations you say that z is the logit regressor but in your model both x and z are used in the negative binomial rather than the bernoulli. Typically you'd use the same predictors (x in this case) in both calls to the negative binomial distribution and use z in a model for the bernoulli parameter theta. To do this, theta doesn't need to be declared as a parameter (just d0 and d1) and then you can construct theta in the model block, since it would be a deterministic function of d0, d1 and the data z. On a related note, I noticed that that the d0 and d1 parameters don't factor into your simulations of the data. I would generate z from a normal distribution and then compute inv_logit(d0 + d1 * z) and use that as the probabilities for the bernoulli in your simulations instead of just taking z from a uniform(0,1).
> >
> > 3) For both theoretical and computational reasons we recommend much tighter priors than normal(0,500), which gives non-negligible weight to values like -1000 and 1000. For your example you probably don't need anything wider than normal(0, 5), and you could probably even go tighter than that.
> >
> > Hope that helps,
> >
> > Jonah
> >
> > On Monday, October 19, 2015 at 2:06:08 PM UTC-4, Kenneth Lowande wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Attempting to implement a zero-inflated negative binomial model, analogous to the zeroinfl() command from the pscl package. Code attached. I'm (very) new to Stan, so any help would be much appreciated.
> >
> >
